title: Clinically / practically relevant or statistical significant?

markdown.headingText: Clinically / practically relevant or statistical significant?
markdown.markdown:
In our analysis of the didgeridoo study, we compared ESS as the average difference between the two groups. Such a comparison is often called an **effect size** or **treatment effect**. It quantifies the observed association between the treatment and outcome, and as such, gives us information about the clinical or practical relevance of the intervention of didgeridoo lessons on the outcome ESS.

Now, if we conducted the didgeridoo study again, even in the same study center and with the same didgeridoo instructor, we would not get exactly the same result, would we? Perhaps it would be close, but it’s unlikely to be exactly the same. We might like to guess what other possible treatment effects would be plausible. For that, we need a **confidence interval** (CI), which describes a range of most plausible treatment effects given our observed data, describing clinical or practical relevance. If a treatment effect corresponding to no difference (e.g. mean difference of 0) is included in the range of the CI, we generally say that the study results are consistent with no difference between the treatment arms.

You may have seen the phrase “95% confidence interval” before. Why can’t we just say “confidence interval”? The “95%” part quantifies *how* confident we want to be that our confidence interval contains the true population-level treatment effect. However, it’s not very often you will see anything except a 95% confidence interval.

Suppose we conduct the same trial 20 times for an intervention that has a true effect of 8 points on the outcome of interest. The plot below shows the estimated treatment effects for each of those studies, as well as the corresponding 95% confidence intervals. From these 20 studies, almost all confidence intervals, that is 19/20 or 95%, contain the true population-level treatment effect, so we can be reasonably confident that the CI we observed from our single trial includes the true effect we would like to estimate.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 12))
library(broom)

simfn <- function(n = 50){
  simdat <- crossing(id = 1:n) |> 
  mutate(trt = rep(0:1, each = n / 2),
          y = rnorm(n(), 30 + trt * 8, 10),
         y = round(y))
  mod <- lm(y ~ trt, data = simdat)
  out <- tidy(mod, conf.int = TRUE) |> 
    filter(term == "trt")
  out
}

set.seed(202612345)
res <- tibble(sim = 1:20,
              n = 50) |> 
  mutate(out = map(n, simfn)) |> 
  unnest(out)

```

Suppose we conduct the same trial 20 times for an intervention that has a true effect of 8 points on the outcome of interest. The plot below shows the estimated treatment effects for each of those studies, as well as the corresponding 95% confidence intervals. From these 20 studies, almost all confidence intervals, that is 19/20 or 95%, contain the true population-level treatment effect, so we can be reasonably confident that the CI we observed from our single trial includes the true effect we would like to estimate.

```{r ci, fig.height = 5, fig.width = 5}
#| echo: false
ggplot(aes(sim, estimate,
           ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high),
       data = res) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 8, color = "blue", linetype = 2) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = NULL) +
  xlab(NULL) + ylab("Estimated treatment effect\nand 95% confidence interval") 

```

And finally, we have **p-values**, a measure of *statistical significance*. Now imagine we have an intervention which does not affect the endpoint compared to the control arm. 

- If the difference is small, and we think that most studies would give us results at least this size or larger (assuming no difference between intervention and control), we say that the results are "not suprising", and conclude no difference. 
- If the difference is large, and we think that few studies would give us results at least this size or larger (assuming no difference between intervention and control), we say that the results are "suprising", and conclude there is a difference between the treatment arms.

P-values quantify how surprised we would be by the results, if we assume that there is no difference between intervention and control. Imagine for a moment that a friend drops by with a 2 sets of 10 dice, giving you the 10 blue dice, and keeping the 10 red dice for himself. "The game is easy. Whoever gets the most 6s out of the 10 dice wins." You roll your blue dice and get exactly one 6s. He rolls his red dice and gets 5 6s! That's amazing! Later you think about it again: if his red dice were fair dice, 5 6s is a really surprising outcome. Was he cheating? How surprising is it exactly, to get 5 6s from a set of 10 fair dice? After a bit of calculation, you discover that getting 5 or more 6s from 10 dice only should happen about 1.5% of the time, assuming you have fair dice. You're not sure, but it looks like he had some sort of special dice, or was very very lucky. Maybe you'll have to get him to try the game again another day to find out which it is.

Back to clinical trials: In regulatory settings, we usually say our level of surprise should be no more than 5% ("significance level"):

- If $p<0.05$, that is, if the observed results would be expected no more than 5% of the time when there is actually no difference between intervention and control, then we say the results are *statistically significant".
- If $p\geq0.05$, that is, if the observed results would be expected more than 5% of the time when there is actually no difference between intervention and control, then we say the results are *not statistically significant".

Power and sample size considerations are generally based on this simple decision rule. In other situations, we do not need clear predefined rules for when the study results are considered "positive". Then it may be more helpful to consider p-values as measures of evidence.

![Instead of reporting a binary yes/no test outcome, the results sections of scientific papers should rather report the exact P-values and interpret that ‘there was no/weak/moderate/strong/very strong evidence’ for a certain finding or effect, depending on approximate ranges into which the actual P-value falls (Muff et al 2022)](images/pvalue_evidence.jpg) 

Regardless of how we interpret p-values, they are measures of statistical significance only, and make no statement about the clinical relevance of the observed results. In very small studies, p-values will be mostly not significant, even if the results are practically meaningful. On the other hand, in very large studies, p-values will generally be significant, even if the observed effects are very small.

For an overview of p-values and confidence intervals, find a good statistical methods textbook (e.g., @kirkwood or @held), or take a look at papers like @rovetta, @greenland or @muff.
